questions.question: Describe the pattern of world population growth from 1 AD to the present, quoting figures from the graph.
questions.expected_answer: Very slow growth from about 250-300 million in 1 AD to about 450-500 million in 1500 and about 1 billion around 1804, with occasional falls (e.g. the Black Death); then increasingly rapid growth: 2 billion in 1927, 3 billion in 1960, 4 billion in 1974, 5 billion in 1987, 6 billion in 1999, 7 billion in 2011 and 8 billion in 2022, with the time to add each billion shrinking. The growth rate peaked at just over 2% a year in the late 1960s and is now just under 1%.

questions.question: Explain why world population grew slowly before 1750 and rapidly afterwards.
questions.expected_answer: Before 1750 both birth and death rates were high (many children died; disease, famine and war killed many), so natural increase was small. After 1750 death rates fell because of better food supply, transport, sanitation and clean water, vaccines and later antibiotics, canned food and refrigeration, while birth rates stayed high, so the gap between births and deaths widened and the population grew rapidly (the demographic transition).

questions.question: Why is world population growth slowing, and where will most future growth occur?
questions.expected_answer: Birth rates and fertility have fallen (from about 5 children per woman in 1950 to about 2.3) because of education especially for girls, family planning, urbanisation, better child survival and pensions. Most future growth will be in Africa, especially sub-Saharan Africa, which has a young population and higher birth rates; Europe and East Asia are ageing and some countries are shrinking.
